cards.question: In C, why is taking the address of a register variable (&x) a compile-time constraint violation even if the compiler spills it to the stack?
cards.answer: The ISO C standard explicitly forbids using & on any identifier declared with register, making it an unconditional compiler error regardless of machine placement.

cards.question: What is the exact difference in pointer arithmetic between arr + 1 and &arr + 1 for int arr[10] (where sizeof(int) == 4)?
cards.answer: arr decays to int*, so arr + 1 advances by 4 bytes (1 element); &arr has type int(*)[10], so &arr + 1 advances by 40 bytes (the entire array).

cards.question: Why does the compiler insert tail padding at the end of a struct in C?
cards.answer: To guarantee that every element in an array of that struct (struct S arr[N]) begins at an address that satisfies the alignment requirement of the largest member.

cards.question: Why does attempting to modify a string literal like char *s = "Hello"; s[0] = 'h'; cause a runtime crash?
cards.answer: String literals reside in the read-only data segment (.rodata); mutating them is undefined behavior and typically causes a segmentation fault.

cards.question: How does setting a pointer to NULL immediately after free(ptr) prevent Use-After-Free (UAF) vulnerabilities?
cards.answer: free() returns memory to the allocator without clearing the pointer or zeroing memory; assigning NULL turns accidental subsequent dereferences into deterministic crashes instead of silent corruption.
